To protect real-time control paths against memory contention, embedded systems implement three structural defenses:

1. *AXI Quality of Service (QoS) Priority Elevation*: The memory interconnect enforces 4-bit `AxQOS` signals, assigning highest priority (`0xF`) to the safety monitor's read channels to enable head-of-line priority preemption over best-effort DMA traffic (`0x0`).
2. *DRAM Bank Partitioning and Page Coloring*: The operating system memory allocator allocates physical memory pages such that real-time safety code and high-rate camera DMA buffers map to strictly disjoint physical DRAM banks, eliminating inter-workload bank conflicts entirely.
3. *On-Chip SRAM Isolation*: Critical safety states, barrier function parameters, and active trajectory splines bypass external DRAM entirely, executing exclusively out of static on-chip SRAM or Data Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM).

## Clock Synchronization and Network Timestamps {#sec-appendix-systems-ptp}

In distributed machine learning clusters, nodes synchronize system clocks via Network Time Protocol (NTP) primarily for coarse event logging and telemetry, while parallel training algorithms synchronize execution through communication barriers (such as NCCL AllReduce). In physical AI systems, however, time directly maps to physical space: when a robot moves at $30\text{ m/s}$, a $1\text{ ms}$ synchronization error produces $3\text{ cm}$ of spatial displacement, warping sensor fusion point clouds and invalidating safety clearance buffers. Distributed perception pipelines must convert sensor timestamps into a common clock domain with a measured conversion-error bound.

### Precision time protocol message exchange

The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) and IEEE 802.1AS (generalized PTP) synchronize a Slave clock ($S$) to a Master clock ($M$) by exchanging four physical timestamps across the communication link:\index{Precision Time Protocol!clock synchronization}\index{Precision Time Protocol!delay measurement}\index{Clock synchronization!PI servo loop}
1. $t_1$: Master transmits a *Sync* frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
2. $t_2$: Slave receives the *Sync* frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.
3. $t_3$: Slave transmits a *Delay_Req* frame, recording its local transmission timestamp.
4. $t_4$: Master receives the *Delay_Req* frame, recording its local arrival timestamp.

Under the assumption of clock stability and symmetric forward and reverse propagation delay ($D_{M \to S} = D_{S \to M} = D$), the time relationships satisfy:
$$ t_2 = t_1 + O + D $$
$$ t_4 = t_3 - O + D $$
where $O$ is the slave-minus-master clock offset. The estimated clock offset is:
$$ O = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) - (t_4 - t_3)}{2} $$
The one-way network propagation delay is:
$$ D = \frac{(t_2 - t_1) + (t_4 - t_3)}{2} $$

**Proportional-Integral (PI) Clock Servo.** Slave clocks adjust their local time base using a closed-loop digital PI servo filter. At synchronization step $k$, the measured offset $O[k]$ drives frequency correction $\Delta f[k]$ applied to the hardware accumulator register:
$$ \Delta f[k] = K_p O[k] + K_i \sum_{j=0}^k O[j] $$
where proportional gain $K_p$ tracks phase error and integral gain $K_i$ eliminates steady-state frequency drift caused by quartz crystal thermal gradient variations.

**Path Asymmetry and Conversion Uncertainty.** If forward and reverse path delays are asymmetric ($\Delta D_{\text{asym}} = D_{M \to S} - D_{S \to M} \ne 0$), the calculated offset incurs an unobservable systematic bias of $\Delta D_{\text{asym}} / 2$. Residual clock uncertainty $\epsilon_{\text{ptp}}$—combining asymmetric propagation, oscillator frequency drift between sync intervals, and hardware timestamp quantization—is explicitly bounded:
$$ \epsilon_{\text{ptp}} \le \frac{|\Delta D_{\text{asym}}|}{2} + \Delta t_{\text{interval}} \cdot \left| \frac{\Delta f}{f_{\text{nom}}} \right| + 2 \tau_{\text{quant}} $$
This conversion bound is stored directly in the proposal header's `sync_error_ns` field (@tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header) and added to every evidence-age calculation in the 1 kHz permission path:
$$ t_{\text{age,max}} = (t_{\text{ctrl}} - t_{\text{evidence}}) + \epsilon_{\text{ptp}} $$

### Physical layer hardware timestamping

Software-based timestamping—where timestamps are captured inside the OS network socket layer or interrupt service routine—suffers from variable kernel queueing, driver interrupt latency, and thread scheduling jitter, injecting $50\,\mu\text{s}$ to $5\text{ ms}$ of non-deterministic timing error.

To eliminate host dispatch error, physical AI hardware utilizes **Physical Layer (PHY) Hardware Timestamping**.[^fn-sys-ptp-timestamps] Dedicated timestamping units in the Ethernet PHY or media access control (MAC) controller capture hardware counter values at the exact instant the physical Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD) crosses the Media Independent Interface (MII / RGMII). This bypasses the entire software stack, reducing timestamping jitter to $< 10\text{ ns}$.

[^fn-sys-ptp-timestamps]: **Hardware Timestamping**\index{Precision Time Protocol!hardware timestamping}: A compatible PHY or MAC timestamps frames closer to the wire than a software interrupt handler. Hardware timestamping removes one source of dispatch variation, while path asymmetry and clock conversion remain. Timestamp uncertainty belongs in the physical belief record and permission budget.

## Heterogeneous SoC Mailboxes, Memory Barriers, and Zero-Copy IPC {#sec-appendix-systems-ipc}

In distributed machine learning systems, inter-process communication occurs across network sockets, gRPC, or direct GPU-to-GPU memory copies over PCIe or NVLink. On heterogeneous robotics SoCs, however, architectures integrate high-performance application processor cores running Linux (hosting deep neural policy inference) with an isolated real-time safety processor (such as an Arm Cortex-R52 or Cortex-M7) on the same silicon die. Communication across this boundary cannot afford kernel-space network protocol overheads or multiple physical memory copies: an uncompressed $4\text{K}$ camera frame ($3840 \times 2160 \times 3\text{ bytes} \approx 24.8\text{ MB}$) transferred at $30\text{ Hz}$ consumes $744\text{ MB/s}$ of bus bandwidth per copy. If an IPC pipeline copies this payload through intermediate kernel socket buffers, memory bandwidth consumption doubles or triples, inducing DRAM bank conflicts and starving real-time control paths.

Consequently, physical AI systems require zero-copy inter-process communication (IPC) frameworks grounded in shared memory, strict publication ordering, and hardware memory barriers across disparate processor cores and GPU accelerators.

### Remote processor messaging over shared SRAM

Communication between Linux application cores and real-time safety microcontrollers relies on shared SRAM mailboxes signaled via hardware doorbells:\index{Inter-core communication!RPMSG framework}\index{Memory barrier!ARM weakly ordered model}

1. Core A (Application Processor) writes a message payload to a fixed buffer in shared SRAM.
2. Core A makes the payload visible to Core B using the platform's coherent mapping or explicit cache maintenance and ordering.
3. Core A triggers an inter-processor interrupt (IPI) by writing to Core B's hardware mailbox register.
4. Core B checks publication order, integrity, age, and permission before using the payload.

Linux [RPMsg](https://docs.kernel.org/staging/rpmsg.html) is a virtio-based messaging framework that may use shared memory and a platform-specific kick. It provides standard transport abstraction but does not prescribe this fixed-buffer protocol or a universal latency bound.

### CPU pipeline reordering and memory fences

In weakly ordered memory architectures (such as ARMv8-A and ARMv9-A), processors do not guarantee that memory writes will be observed by other cores in program order. Out-of-order execution engines and asynchronous write buffers can reorder stores to non-dependent addresses:
```c
// Core A (Application Processor); q_target and q_cmd are joint_target_t structs
shared_buffer->q_target = q_cmd; // Store 1: Payload (struct copy)
mailbox_doorbell = 1;            // Store 2: Interrupt trigger
```
If the CPU reorders Store 2 ahead of Store 1, Core B receives the interrupt before the new joint target is committed to physical memory, reading stale or torn data.

**Hardware Memory Barriers and Shareability Domains.** To enforce deterministic ordering across heterogeneous cores, developers must insert architectural memory barriers:\index{Memory barrier!instruction ordering}\index{Memory barrier!DMB vs DSB vs ISB}
```c
shared_buffer->q_target = q_cmd; // Struct copy of the joint targets
__asm__ volatile("dmb oshst" ::: "memory"); // Outer-shareable store barrier
mailbox_doorbell = 1;            // Assert doorbell register
```
In ARM architectures, memory barriers and instructions are distinguished by scope and execution semantics:

* `DMB` (Data Memory Barrier): Ensures that memory accesses specified before the barrier appear in memory before memory accesses specified after the barrier. It does not block execution of non-memory instructions.
* `DSB` (Data Synchronization Barrier): A stricter barrier that halts CPU pipeline instruction dispatch until all previous memory transactions and bus buffer flushes have completed.
* `ISB` (Instruction Synchronization Barrier): Flushes the CPU instruction prefetch pipeline, ensuring subsequent instructions are fetched anew from cache or memory.

Barriers operate across explicit architectural **shareability domains**:

* `DMB ISHST` (Inner Shareable Store): Orders stores across cores within the local application CPU cluster sharing a coherent L2/L3 cache.
* `DMB OSHST` / `DMB OSH` (Outer Shareable): Enforces ordering across the entire system-on-chip, including the real-time Cortex-R/M cores, GPU, and DMA subsystems.
* `DMB SY` (System): Enforces ordering across all system masters and peripherals on the SoC.

*Cache Maintenance vs. Non-Cacheable Mappings.* If shared SRAM is mapped as Normal Cacheable memory, Core A must explicitly clean the cache line to the Point of Coherency (`DC CVAC`) before asserting the doorbell, and Core B must invalidate its local cache line (`DC IVAC`) before reading. Because cache clean and invalidate operations require hundreds of CPU cycles and are vulnerable to eviction timing bugs, real-time shared SRAM mailboxes are typically mapped as **Normal Non-Cacheable** (or Device-nGnRnE) memory. Under Non-Cacheable mappings, cache maintenance operations are eliminated entirely, and store barriers (`DMB OSHST`) guarantee single-cycle order enforcement across write buffers. Furthermore, shared mailbox structures must be aligned to cache-line boundaries (`alignas(64)`) to prevent false sharing and atomic cache-line bouncing. See @sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges and @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die for heterogeneous SoC communication architectures and isolation guarantees.[^fn-sys-memory-barriers]

### POSIX shared memory and lock-free SPSC ring buffers

Within user-space Linux runtimes, independent operating system processes (such as a vision preprocessing daemon, a multimodal VLA policy inference server, and a high-rate state estimator) exchange telemetry and sensor streams without kernel socket copies via **POSIX Shared Memory** (`shm_open` and `mmap`):\index{Shared memory!POSIX shm}\index{Concurrency!lock-free SPSC ring buffer}

1. A producer process creates a POSIX shared memory object using `shm_open("/robot_telemetry", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0660)` located in the RAM-backed `tmpfs` filesystem (`/dev/shm`).
2. Sizing the segment via `ftruncate(fd, sizeof(telemetry_ring_buffer_t))` allocates physical pages.
3. Both producer and consumer processes map the memory into their respective virtual address spaces via `mmap(NULL, sizeof(...), PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0)`.
4. Crucially, each process immediately invokes `mlock()` on the mapped region, guaranteeing that the shared pages remain pinned in physical RAM and cannot trigger demand page faults during execution.

**Lock-Free Single-Producer Single-Consumer (SPSC) Ring Buffers.** When streaming sequential sensor frames or trajectory waypoints across processes, mutual-exclusion mutexes introduce non-deterministic blocking and priority inversion. A lock-free SPSC ring buffer coordinates communication using atomic head and tail pointers with explicit acquire-release semantics:

```cpp
#include <atomic>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstddef>
#include <new>

template <typename T, size_t Capacity>
class LockFreeSpscRingBuffer {
    static_assert((Capacity & (Capacity - 1)) == 0, "Capacity must be a power of two");

private:
    // Align head and tail to distinct 64-byte cache lines to eliminate false sharing
    alignas(64) std::atomic<uint64_t> write_index_{0};
    alignas(64) std::atomic<uint64_t> read_index_{0};
    alignas(64) T storage_[Capacity];

public:
    bool Push(const T& item) {
        const uint64_t current_write = write_index_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        const uint64_t current_read = read_index_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);

        if (current_write - current_read >= Capacity) {
            return false; // Buffer full: non-blocking drop or backpressure
        }

        // Fast bitwise masking replacing expensive modulo division
        storage_[current_write & (Capacity - 1)] = item;

        // Release order ensures item stores are committed before advancing pointer
        write_index_.store(current_write + 1, std::memory_order_release);
        return true;
    }

    bool Pop(T& item) {
        const uint64_t current_read = read_index_.load(std::memory_order_relaxed);
        const uint64_t current_write = write_index_.load(std::memory_order_acquire);

        if (current_read == current_write) {
            return false; // Buffer empty
        }

        item = storage_[current_read & (Capacity - 1)];

        // Release order publishes free slot back to producer
        read_index_.store(current_read + 1, std::memory_order_release);
        return true;
    }
};
```

By separating `write_index_` and `read_index_` onto distinct 64-byte cache lines (`alignas(64)`), this data structure guarantees that the producer's atomic increments never invalidate the consumer's private L1 cache line, completely eliminating MESI cache line bouncing.

### Multi-rate synchronization: Double-buffering versus triple-buffering

In cyber-physical machines, producer and consumer tasks rarely execute at the same frequency. A multimodal vision-language-action policy may produce candidate trajectory chunks at $20\text{ Hz}$ ($50\text{ ms}$ period) with variable inference jitter ($\pm 15\text{ ms}$), while the downstream safety permission filter and motor tracking loop execute strictly at $1\text{ kHz}$ ($1\text{ ms}$ period).\index{Concurrency!double-buffering}\index{Concurrency!triple-buffering}\index{Multi-rate synchronization!wait-free buffers}

**The Limitations of Double-Buffering.** In a standard double-buffering architecture, memory is split into a front buffer (read by consumer) and a back buffer (written by producer):

* If the reader and writer synchronize via a lock or flip-flag, the high-frequency $1\text{ kHz}$ consumer must stall whenever the $20\text{ Hz}$ producer is in the middle of writing a multi-kilobyte trajectory payload, violating the consumer's $1\text{ ms}$ hard real-time deadline.
* If the consumer does not wait, it either reads partially written, torn memory or is forced to continue re-reading stale data across dozens of cycles without knowing whether an update was attempted.

**Triple-Buffering Protocol.** To achieve completely non-blocking, wait-free, zero-copy, and tear-free state transfer across asynchronous clock domains, physical AI systems employ **triple-buffering**:

1. *Buffer Pool*: Three preallocated buffers of identical geometry:
   - Buffer $A$: Owned exclusively by the Producer (active write buffer).
   - Buffer $B$: Owned exclusively by the Consumer (active read buffer).
   - Buffer $C$: Shared intermediate buffer (holds the most recent complete, validated state).
2. *State Exchange Register*: A single 32-bit atomic word encapsulates two 8-bit buffer indices (`latest_written_index` and `reader_current_index`) and a 1-bit `new_data_available` flag.
3. *Producer Write Step*:
   - The producer writes its new trajectory chunk into its private buffer without synchronization.
   - Upon completion, it commits the payload with a memory barrier (`std::memory_order_release`).
   - The producer atomically exchanges its buffer pointer with the intermediate buffer pointer in a single lock-free compare-and-swap (CAS) instruction and sets `new_data_available = 1`.
   - The producer now owns the previous intermediate buffer as its new private back buffer.
4. *Consumer Read Step*:
   - At the beginning of its $1\text{ kHz}$ tick, the consumer inspects the atomic exchange register via `std::memory_order_acquire`.
   - If `new_data_available == 1`, the consumer atomically swaps its private buffer pointer with the intermediate buffer pointer and clears the flag.
   - The consumer now reads the freshly promoted buffer in complete isolation.
   - If `new_data_available == 0`, the consumer retains its existing buffer without stalling.

Under triple-buffering, neither producer nor consumer ever blocks or spins on a lock. The reader is guaranteed $\mathcal{O}(1)$ deterministic latency ($< 50\text{ ns}$ pointer swap), and the payload is never torn, providing optimal multi-rate temporal decoupling.

### CUDA inter-process communication for multi-accelerator pipelines

On high-throughput robotics platforms (such as autonomous mobile robots equipped with multiple GMSL2 camera clusters and lidar arrays), raw perception data streams into accelerator GPU memory for tensor processing. In modular physical AI software architectures, perception preprocessing (e.g., optical flow, spatial unprojection, and feature extraction) and foundation policy inference often execute in separate Linux processes for fault containment. Passing multi-gigabyte tensor buffers between processes via host system RAM consumes tens of gigabytes per second of shared DRAM bandwidth, precipitating memory bus contention.\index{CUDA!Inter-Process Communication}\index{CUDA IPC!zero-copy tensor sharing}\index{Peer-to-peer DMA!accelerator IPC}

To eliminate host DRAM staging entirely, **CUDA Inter-Process Communication (CUDA IPC)** enables direct peer-to-peer GPU memory access across distinct Linux process address spaces:

```c
// Process A (Perception Producer): Export GPU device memory handle
float *d_camera_tensor;
cudaMalloc(&d_camera_tensor, TENSOR_BYTES);

// Allocate and capture an opaque 64-byte IPC memory handle
cudaIpcMemHandle_t ipc_mem_handle;
cudaIpcGetMemHandle(&ipc_mem_handle, (void *)d_camera_tensor);

// Send the 64-byte handle to Process B via POSIX shm or UNIX domain socket
send_ipc_handle_to_consumer(&ipc_mem_handle);
```

In Process B (Policy Consumer), the exported handle is mapped directly into its local GPU virtual address space without copying:

```c
// Process B (Policy Consumer): Map exported GPU memory directly
cudaIpcMemHandle_t received_handle;
receive_ipc_handle_from_producer(&received_handle);

float *d_mapped_tensor;
cudaIpcOpenMemHandle((void **)&d_mapped_tensor, received_handle,
                     cudaIpcMemLazyEnablePeerAccess);

// Launch inference kernel directly referencing Process A's physical GPU memory
launch_vla_encoder_kernel<<<grid, block, 0, compute_stream>>>(d_mapped_tensor);

// Clean up mapping upon pipeline shutdown
cudaIpcCloseMemHandle((void *)d_mapped_tensor);
```

**Cross-Process CUDA Event Synchronization.** To synchronize GPU execution across processes without round-tripping to host CPU threads, CUDA IPC exports GPU hardware synchronization primitives via `cudaIpcGetEventHandle()` and `cudaIpcOpenEventHandle()`. Process A records an event in hardware (`cudaEventRecord(event, producer_stream)`). Process B imports the event handle and enqueues a hardware barrier on its local stream:
$$ \text{cudaStreamWaitEvent}(\text{consumer\_stream}, \text{imported\_event}, 0) $$
The GPU's on-chip hardware work distributor halts execution of `consumer_stream` until Process A's preprocessing kernel completes in silicon. This achieves microsecond-scale cross-process coordination across PCIe and NVLink interconnects with zero CPU host involvement and zero memory copy overhead.

[^fn-sys-memory-barriers]: **Hardware Memory Barriers**\index{Memory barrier!instruction ordering}: Barriers order accesses only within their specified shareability and memory-attribute contract. On a noncoherent route, cache clean/invalidate operations or coherent mappings are also required. [Arm's memory-ordering guide](https://developer.arm.com/community/arm-community-blogs/b/architectures-and-processors-blog/posts/memory-access-ordering-part-3---memory-access-ordering-in-the-arm-architecture) distinguishes ordering from coherence.

## Actuator Electrical and Thermal Dynamics {#sec-appendix-systems-actuators}

In reinforcement learning and simulation environments (such as MuJoCo or Isaac Gym), policy actions are typically abstracted as instantaneous torque or position commands applied at discrete simulation steps. In physical systems, however, actuators convert electrical energy into mechanical work through electromagnetic Lorentz forces, subject to coupled electrical, thermal, and kinematic constraints.

### Stator electrical rise time

A brushless permanent-magnet synchronous motor (PMSM / BLDC) phase winding exhibits phase resistance $R_{\text{phase}}$ and phase inductance $L_{\text{phase}}$. Applying terminal voltage $V_{\text{terminal}}$ against back-electromotive force $e_{\text{bemf}} = K_e \omega_m$ yields the first-order stator current ODE:\index{Actuator!electrical rise time}\index{Field-Oriented Control!dq-frame dynamics}
$$ L_{\text{phase}} \frac{dI(t)}{dt} + R_{\text{phase}} I(t) = V_{\text{terminal}} - K_e \omega_m $$

In three-phase synchronous machines under Field-Oriented Control (FOC), the stator currents are transformed from the three-phase $abc$ frame into the orthogonal rotor synchronous $dq$ reference frame via the Clarke and Park transformations:
$$ V_d = R_{\text{phase}} I_d + L_d \frac{dI_d}{dt} - \omega_e L_q I_q $$
$$ V_q = R_{\text{phase}} I_q + L_q \frac{dI_q}{dt} + \omega_e L_d I_d + \omega_e \lambda_{\text{pm}} $$
where $\omega_e = p \omega_m$ is electrical angular velocity ($p$ pole pairs), $\lambda_{\text{pm}}$ is the rotor permanent-magnet flux linkage, and $L_d, L_q$ are direct and quadrature axis inductances. Under standard constant torque-angle control ($I_d = 0$), electromagnetic torque is directly proportional to quadrature current:
$$ \tau_{\text{motor}} = \frac{3}{2} p \, \lambda_{\text{pm}} I_q = K_t I_q $$

For a commanded voltage step applied from rest ($\omega_m = 0$), quadrature current rises exponentially:
$$ I_q(t) = \frac{V_{\text{terminal}}}{R_{\text{phase}}} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_e} \right), \quad \tau_e = \frac{L_q}{R_{\text{phase}}} $$
where $\tau_e$ is the electrical time constant. Current—and therefore delivered torque—reaches approximately 63 percent of its steady-state value after one time constant $\tau_e$ (typically $200\,\mu\text{s}$ to $2\text{ ms}$ in robotics actuators). An unprivileged neural policy step command cannot produce an instantaneous step in physical torque.

Furthermore, achievable current is constrained by inverter voltage saturation:
$$ \sqrt{V_d^2 + V_q^2} \le \frac{V_{\text{bus}}}{\sqrt{3}} $$
As rotor speed $\omega_m$ rises, back-EMF $\omega_e \lambda_{\text{pm}}$ increases, consuming available quadrature voltage $V_q$. At the actuator's base speed, voltage headroom vanishes, and torque collapses unless negative direct-axis current ($I_d < 0$, flux weakening) is commanded to demagnetize the stator air gap.

### Lumped thermal networks and stator Joule heating

Current flowing through stator windings dissipates resistive Joule heat:
$$ P_{\text{loss}}(t) = \frac{3}{2} I_q^2(t) R_{\text{phase}}(T) $$
where copper electrical resistance increases linearly with temperature:
$$ R_{\text{phase}}(T) = R_0 \left[ 1 + \alpha_{\text{Cu}} (T - T_0) \right] $$
with temperature coefficient $\alpha_{\text{Cu}} \approx 0.00393\text{ K}^{-1}$ for copper. At an operating temperature of $150^\circ\text{C}$, stator copper resistance is approximately $50\text{ percent}$ higher than at room temperature ($25^\circ\text{C}$). To sustain the same commanded torque $\tau = K_t I_q$, the motor requires identical current $I_q$ but generates $50\text{ percent}$ more thermal dissipation, creating positive feedback between winding temperature and Joule heating that accelerates thermal degradation.

**Multi-Node Lumped Thermal Networks.** In a physical motor, thermal dynamics span multiple physical interfaces with disparate thermal masses:\index{Actuator!stator thermal dynamics}\index{Actuator!thermal ladder network}

1. *Stator Winding Copper*: Low thermal capacitance $C_{\text{cu}}$, rapid heating from Joule dissipation ($\tau_{\text{cu}} \sim 10\text{--}30\text{ s}$).
2. *Stator Iron Laminations*: Moderate thermal capacitance $C_{\text{iron}}$, absorbing iron eddy-current and hysteresis losses $P_{\text{iron}} \propto \omega_e^{1.5} B^2$ and heat conducted across winding insulation $R_{\text{th,cu-iron}}$.
3. *Motor Frame and Aluminum Housing*: Large thermal capacitance $C_{\text{case}}$, conducting heat into the robotic link structure and convecting to ambient air through $R_{\text{th,case-amb}}$ ($\tau_{\text{case}} \sim 10\text{--}30\text{ min}$).

The temperature dynamics across these nodes satisfy the coupled differential system:
$$ C_{\text{cu}} \frac{dT_{\text{cu}}}{dt} = P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{T_{\text{cu}} - T_{\text{iron}}}{R_{\text{th,cu-iron}}} $$
$$ C_{\text{iron}} \frac{dT_{\text{iron}}}{dt} = \frac{T_{\text{cu}} - T_{\text{iron}}}{R_{\text{th,cu-iron}}} + P_{\text{iron}} - \frac{T_{\text{iron}} - T_{\text{case}}}{R_{\text{th,iron-case}}} $$
$$ C_{\text{case}} \frac{dT_{\text{case}}}{dt} = \frac{T_{\text{iron}} - T_{\text{case}}}{R_{\text{th,iron-case}}} - \frac{T_{\text{case}} - T_{\text{ambient}}}{R_{\text{th,case-amb}}} $$

In a simplified single-node lumped thermal model with effective thermal resistance to ambient $\theta_{JA}$ (in $\text{K/W}$) and thermal heat capacity $C_{\text{th}}$ (in $\text{J/K}$), temperature rise $\Delta T(t) = T_{\text{winding}}(t) - T_{\text{ambient}}$ satisfies:[^fn-sys-motor-heating]
$$ C_{\text{th}} \frac{d\Delta T(t)}{dt} = P_{\text{loss}}(t) - \frac{\Delta T(t)}{\theta_{JA}} $$
Under constant power, temperature rises with thermal time constant $\tau_{\text{th}} = \theta_{JA} C_{\text{th}}$:
$$ \Delta T(t) = P_{\text{loss}} \theta_{JA} \left( 1 - e^{-t / \tau_{\text{th}}} \right) $$

**Continuous Torque vs. Transient Overdrive.** Continuous torque capacity $\tau_{\text{cont}}$ is bounded by the maximum allowable winding temperature rise $\Delta T_{\max}$:
$$ \tau_{\text{cont}} \le K_t \sqrt{\frac{\Delta T_{\max}}{\theta_{JA} R_{\text{phase}}}} $$
Transient torque peaks $\tau_{\text{peak}} \approx 2\text{--}4 \times \tau_{\text{cont}}$ are permitted during aggressive dynamic maneuvers only if an active digital $I^2 t$ thermal protection observer running on the safety microcontroller bounds the thermal integral:
$$ \Delta T[k+1] = \Delta T[k] e^{-\Delta t / \tau_{\text{th}}} + \theta_{JA} P_{\text{loss}}[k] \left( 1 - e^{-\Delta t / \tau_{\text{th}}} \right) $$
When estimated winding temperature approaches the dielectric breakdown limit ($180^\circ\text{C}$ Class H insulation) or rotor neodymium magnet demagnetization threshold ($80\text{--}120^\circ\text{C}$), the permission filter clamps commanded current, preventing catastrophic actuator destruction.

[^fn-sys-motor-heating]: **Stator Thermal Time Constants**\index{Actuator!stator thermal dynamics}: Resistive Joule heating elevates motor phase winding temperatures during continuous high-torque maneuvers. Because copper electrical resistivity increases linearly with temperature, hot windings exhibit higher resistance, reducing torque output under terminal voltage saturation. Exceeding winding insulation temperature limits breaks down dielectric coatings, causing inter-turn short circuits and irreversible actuator destruction.

### Reflected rotor inertia and angular jerk limits {#sec-appendix-systems-rotor-jerk}

Geared electromagnetic actuators amplify delivered motor torque while multiplying rotor inertia at the joint output. For a transmission with gear reduction ratio $N = \omega_{\text{motor}} / \omega_{\text{joint}}$, kinetic energy conservation dictates the reflected inertia acting at the output link:\index{Reflected rotor inertia!kinetic energy derivation}\index{Angular jerk!electromechanical limits}
$$ E_k = \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{rotor}} \omega_{\text{motor}}^2 + \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{load}} \omega_{\text{joint}}^2 = \frac{1}{2} (J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}) \dot{q}^2 $$
The effective rotational inertia seen at joint coordinate $q$ is:
$$ J_{\text{eff}} = J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}} $$
The joint equation of motion under motor electromagnetic torque $\tau_{\text{motor}}$ is:
$$ \ddot{q} = \frac{N \tau_{\text{motor}} - \tau_{\text{ext}}}{J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}} $$
Differentiating $\ddot{q}$ with respect to gear ratio $N$ at zero external load yields:
$$ \frac{\partial \ddot{q}}{\partial N} = \frac{\tau_{\text{motor}} (J_{\text{load}} - N^2 J_{\text{rotor}})}{(J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}})^2} $$
Setting $\frac{\partial \ddot{q}}{\partial N} = 0$ yields the **inertia-matching ratio** $N^* = \sqrt{J_{\text{load}} / J_{\text{rotor}}}$. When $N > N^*$, counter-intuitively, increasing the gear ratio decreases delivered joint acceleration because the motor spends the majority of its torque accelerating its own rotor rather than the link.

#### Dynamic angular jerk and torque slew limits

Angular jerk $j_{\text{joint}}(t) = \dddot{q}(t)$ measures the time rate of change of joint acceleration:
$$ j_{\text{joint}}(t) = \frac{N}{J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}}} \frac{d\tau_{\text{motor}}(t)}{dt} $$
Electromagnetic torque relates to stator quadrature current via torque constant $K_t$: $\tau_{\text{motor}} = K_t I_q$. From the stator electrical dynamics in this section, current slew rate is bounded by winding inductance $L_{\text{phase}}$:
$$ \frac{d\tau_{\text{motor}}}{dt} = K_t \frac{dI_q}{dt} = \frac{K_t}{L_{\text{phase}}} \left( V_{\text{terminal}} - K_e \omega_m - R_{\text{phase}} I_q \right) $$
Under maximum DC bus terminal voltage saturation $V_{\max}$, the physical upper bound on delivered angular jerk is:
$$ |j_{\max}| \le \frac{N K_t (V_{\max} - K_e \omega_m)}{L_{\text{phase}} (J_{\text{load}} + N^2 J_{\text{rotor}})} $$
When an unprivileged neural policy outputs a step torque discontinuity $\Delta \boldsymbol{\tau}$ across discrete timesteps, the commanded derivative $\frac{d\tau}{dt} \to \infty$ cannot be delivered instantaneously by physical silicon. The inverter enters hard voltage saturation, causing steep current slew ($dI/dt$), intense thermal stress on power MOSFETs, and shock loads across gear-tooth contact flanks ($\sigma_b \propto W_t / (b m Y)$). Synchronous pre-actuation invariant filters evaluate numerical torque derivatives $(\boldsymbol{\tau}[k] - \boldsymbol{\tau}[k-1]) / \Delta t$ to ensure requested actions remain within allowable jerk envelopes before latching power stages.

## DC Bus Power Distribution and Energy Absorption {#sec-appendix-systems-power}

In data center machine learning clusters, electrical power is managed by high-capacity facility uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and dedicated substation transformers. On mobile autonomous platforms, computational accelerators and mechanical actuators draw from a shared, finite DC power distribution network. A robotic platform's electrical power distribution network must supply acceleration surges and absorb regenerative braking energy across finite bus capacitance and harness impedance.

### Inductive droop and capacitive decoupling

When multiple high-torque actuators accelerate simultaneously (such as a humanoid jumping or an articulated arm bracing against an unexpected payload), total load current steps by $\Delta I_{\text{load}} = \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\text{axes}}} \Delta I_k$ with steep current slew rates $dI_{\text{load}}/dt \sim 10^5\text{--}10^6\text{ A/s}$. The electrical wiring harness connecting the main battery to distributed joint inverters possesses parasitic loop inductance $L_{\text{bus}}$ (typically $1\text{--}5\,\mu\text{H}$ for a 1-meter harness) and harness resistance $R_{\text{bus}}$. These parasitics impede source current delivery, producing instantaneous inductive rail droop at the actuator inverter terminals:\index{Inductive voltage droop!DC bus harness}\index{Decoupling capacitors!inverter DC bus}\index{Under-Voltage Lockout!gate driver protection}
$$ \Delta V_{\text{bus}}(t) = R_{\text{bus}} I_{\text{source}}(t) + L_{\text{bus}} \frac{dI_{\text{source}}}{dt} + \Delta V_C(t) $$
Local inverter bus capacitance $C_{\text{bus}}$ must supply the instantaneous charge deficit between load demand and battery source current:
$$ \Delta V_C(t) = \frac{1}{C_{\text{bus}}} \int_0^t \left( I_{\text{load}}(s) - I_{\text{source}}(s) \right) ds $$

**Under-Voltage Lockout (UVLO).** If the DC bus terminal voltage drops below the drive's configured Under-Voltage Lockout threshold $V_{\text{UVLO}}$ (e.g., $18\text{ V}$ on a $24\text{ V}$ nominal bus, or $36\text{ V}$ on a $48\text{ V}$ bus), the gate driver IC enters UVLO fault protection, disabling gate bias within microseconds to prevent power MOSFETs from operating in their linear resistive region. This instantly drops motor torque to zero, causing the joint to collapse under gravity.

To maintain DC bus stability during a step acceleration of duration $\Delta t_{\text{step}}$, the minimum local decoupling capacitance is bounded by:
$$ C_{\text{bus}} \ge \frac{\Delta I_{\text{step}} \cdot \Delta t_{\text{step}}}{2 \Delta V_{\text{droop, max}}} $$
Local capacitor banks combine low-ESR multi-layer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) for high-frequency ripple filtering ($20\text{--}100\text{ kHz}$ inverter switching) with bulk electrolytic or polymer capacitors for transient step energy buffering. Furthermore, the capacitor bank must be rated for RMS ripple current:
$$ I_{\text{rms,ripple}} \approx I_{\text{phase}} \sqrt{2 D \left( 1 - \frac{4}{3} D \right)} $$
preventing internal capacitor overheating from equivalent series resistance ($I^2 \cdot \text{ESR}$).

### Regenerative braking surges and chopper sizing

During controlled regenerative deceleration or emergency stopping, mechanical kinetic energy $E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ (linear platform motion) or $E_k = \frac{1}{2} J_{\text{eff}} \dot{q}^2$ (articulated joint rotation) is converted back into electrical energy by the motor acting as a generator. Current flows back through the inverter bridge into the DC bus via active synchronous rectification or freewheeling body diodes.\index{Regenerative braking!chopper resistor}\index{Power electronics!brake chopper}\index{Brake chopper!hysteresis control}

If the battery cannot accept this regenerative current—such as when the battery pack is at 100 percent state-of-charge ($> 4.2\text{ V/cell}$), when battery internal resistance rises at freezing temperatures, or when safety contactors open to isolate the pack—the returned electrical energy $\eta_{\text{regen}} E_k$ is forced into the local bus capacitor $C_{\text{bus}}$. The resulting terminal voltage surge follows the ideal capacitor relationship:
$$ \Delta E_C = \frac{1}{2} C_{\text{bus}} \left( V_{\text{final}}^2 - V_{\text{initial}}^2 \right) = \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k $$
$$ V_{\text{final}} = \sqrt{ V_{\text{initial}}^2 + \frac{2 \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k}{C_{\text{bus}}} } $$

If $V_{\text{final}}$ exceeds the MOSFET drain-source breakdown voltage $V_{\text{DSS}}$ or the inverter Over-Voltage Lockout (OVLO) threshold, the power semiconductors enter destructive avalanche breakdown.

**Dynamic Brake Choppers.** To prevent overvoltage destruction, motor drives incorporate an active **dynamic brake chopper**. When DC bus voltage crosses a hardware clamp threshold $V_{\text{clamp,on}}$, a high-power semiconductor switch (MOSFET or IGBT) modulates an auxiliary low-inductance braking resistor $R_{\text{brake}}$ with hysteresis:[^fn-sys-brake-chopper]
$$ R_{\text{brake}} \le \frac{V_{\text{clamp}}^2}{P_{\text{regen, peak}}} $$
$$ P_{\text{regen, peak}} \approx \eta_{\text{regen}} \cdot \tau_{\text{brake}} \cdot \omega_{\max} $$
The chopper comparator switches the resistor on when $V_{\text{bus}} \ge V_{\text{clamp,on}}$ and turns off when $V_{\text{bus}} \le V_{\text{clamp,off}}$, preventing rapid oscillation. In addition to peak power sizing, the braking resistor must be rated for single-pulse adiabatic energy absorption:
$$ E_{\text{pulse}} \ge \eta_{\text{regen}} E_k $$
with a thermal cooldown time constant that prevents cumulative thermal failure during repeated stop-and-go duty cycles.

[^fn-sys-brake-chopper]: **Dynamic Braking Choppers**\index{Regenerative braking!chopper resistor}: A qualified chopper can dissipate returned energy when the battery is unavailable as a sink. Its threshold, switch and resistor ratings, pulse duration, and thermal recovery must be tested. Regeneration and chopper operation are not inherent to every emergency stop; safe torque off can instead leave a motor coasting.

## Real-Time Fieldbuses and Lock-Free Synchronization {#sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus}

In distributed machine learning clusters, networks are built on high-bandwidth fabrics (such as 100/400 Gbps RoCEv2 or InfiniBand) optimized for aggregate data-parallel throughput via credit-based flow control. In physical AI systems, however, the onboard communication fabric must simultaneously multiplex two diametrically opposed traffic classes:

1. *High-bandwidth best-effort perception streams*: Multi-gigabit video from high-resolution GMSL2/GigE Vision cameras ($2\text{--}8\text{ Gbps}$) and 3D lidar point clouds ($100\text{--}1000\text{ Mbps}$) streaming into the AI accelerator's unified memory for foundation model inference.
2. *Hard real-time periodic control traffic*: Deterministic 1 kHz joint setpoint commands and high-resolution torque/position feedback ($100\text{--}500\text{ kbps}$) exchanged with distributed motor inverters.

If these two traffic classes share a naive best-effort Ethernet fabric with first-in, first-out (FIFO) queueing, multi-megabyte perception bursts cause severe queue congestion and buffer bloat. A burst of video frames can delay a motor control packet by $5\text{--}20\text{ ms}$—violating the 1 ms control deadline, starving the inverter current loop, and tripping hardware emergency stops. Coordinating distributed drives while ingesting perception streams requires an architectural separation of fabrics, deterministic bus schedules, and bounded lock-free publication protocols.

### Fieldbus serialization and schedulability

On shared physical buses, $N_{\text{axes}}$ actuator drives transmit telemetry and receive setpoints cyclically. To prevent perception traffic from corrupting motor timing, physical AI architectures utilize dedicated deterministic fieldbuses (CAN 2.0B, CAN-FD, or EtherCAT) or time-scheduled switched Ethernet (IEEE TSN).\index{Fieldbus!CAN 2.0B arbitration}\index{Fieldbus!CAN-FD arbitration}\index{Fieldbus!CAN-FD WCRT}\index{Fieldbus!EtherCAT on-the-fly}\index{Fieldbus!TSN perception-control multiplexing}

**CAN 2.0B Classical Serial Bus.** Classical Controller Area Network (CAN 2.0B, ISO 11898-1) utilizes differential signaling over a shielded twisted pair ($V_{\text{CANH}} - V_{\text{CANL}} \approx 2.0\text{ V}$ for dominant logic 0, and $0\text{ V}$ for recessive logic 1):

* *Arbitration Mechanics*: Nodes access the physical medium using non-destructive bitwise arbitration. When two nodes transmit simultaneously, a dominant bit overrides a recessive bit. A node transmitting a recessive bit that samples a dominant bit on the physical bus immediately ceases transmission and yields the bus to the higher-priority frame without message corruption.
* *Framing and Payload Constraints*: Standard CAN 2.0B frames support either an 11-bit standard or 29-bit extended identifier, with payload length strictly capped at $B_{\text{payload}} \le 8\text{ bytes}$ via a 4-bit Data Length Code (DLC).
* *Bit-Stuffing and Latency*: To preserve transceiver phase-locked loop (PLL) clock synchronization, the physical layer inserts an opposite stuff bit after every 5 consecutive identical bits in the arbitration and data fields. On a $1\text{ Mbps}$ bus, an 8-byte frame (containing approximately 108 to 130 bits depending on stuff-bit insertion) requires $108\text{--}130\,\mu\text{s}$ to serialize:
$$ t_{\text{frame,CAN2.0B}} \approx \frac{47 + 8 B_{\text{payload}} + \lfloor (34 + 8 B_{\text{payload}} - 1) / 4 \rfloor}{R_{\text{bit}}} $$
* *The Scalability Bottleneck*: On a $1\text{ ms}$ ($1000\,\mu\text{s}$) control cycle, a single CAN 2.0B bus operating at $1\text{ Mbps}$ can transport at most 6 to 7 messages before exceeding $80\text{ percent}$ bus load, above which arbitration queueing delays diverge. Servicing a modern 30-axis humanoid robot would require at least 5 to 6 independent physical CAN buses, creating severe wiring harness bulk and complex multi-bus gateway synchronization overheads.

**CAN-FD Dual-Rate Bit Timing and Arbitration.** Controller Area Network with Flexible Data-Rate (CAN-FD, ISO 11898-1:2015) overcomes the payload and bandwidth limits of classical CAN through dual bit-rate switching and payload expansion up to 64 bytes:

* *Arbitration Phase*: Transmitted at the nominal bit rate $R_{\text{nom}}$ (typically $500\text{ kbps}$ or $1\text{ Mbps}$). The bit time $T_{\text{bit,nom}} = 1/R_{\text{nom}}$ must accommodate physical cable propagation delays across the robot chassis and transceiver delays ($2 t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{transceiver}}$), allowing non-destructive bitwise priority arbitration. Nodes drive the bus using dominant or recessive states. If two nodes transmit simultaneously, the lower numerical message identifier (higher logical priority) overwrites recessive bits, winning the bus without collision or frame destruction.
* *Data Phase*: Once arbitration is established, the winning node asserts the Bit Rate Switch (BRS) bit, accelerating transmission to the data bit rate $R_{\text{data}}$ (typically $2\text{--}8\text{ Mbps}$). Because only a single node drives the bus during the data phase, physical propagation delay between distributed nodes no longer constrains bit duration.
* *Bit-Stuffing Overhead*: Dynamic stuff bits are inserted after 5 consecutive identical bits in arbitration, while the CRC field incorporates fixed stuff bits with an explicit stuff count. In the worst-case bit pattern, bit stuffing can inflate frame transmission duration by up to $20\text{ percent}$.

The serialization duration for frame $i$ is:
$$ t_{\text{frame},i} \approx \frac{B_{\text{arb},i}}{R_{\text{nom}}} + \frac{B_{\text{data},i}}{R_{\text{data}}} + t_{\text{stuff},i} + t_{\text{interframe},i} $$
where $B_{\text{arb},i}$ is the arbitration field length (identifier, control bits), $B_{\text{data},i}$ is the payload and CRC length, $t_{\text{stuff},i}$ accounts for stuff bits, and $t_{\text{interframe},i}$ is the minimum 3-bit inter-frame spacing.

**CAN-FD Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT).** Because CAN-FD frames are non-preemptive—a transmission in progress cannot be aborted when a higher-priority message is released—the worst-case response time $R_i$ of periodic control frame $i$ is evaluated via Tindell's recurrence:
$$ R_i = C_i + B_i + \sum_{j \in hp(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i + J_j + \tau_{\text{bit}}}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j $$
where $C_i = t_{\text{frame},i}$, $J_j$ is the release jitter of higher-priority message $j$, and $B_i$ is the maximum lower-priority blocking duration:
$$ B_i = \max_{k \in lp(i)} C_k $$
Because a maximum 64-byte CAN-FD frame at $2\text{ Mbps}$ requires approximately $300\text{--}400\,\mu\text{s}$ to serialize, a CAN-FD bus at $80\text{ percent}$ utilization can service at most $10\text{--}15$ joint axes at 1 kHz. CAN-FD cannot carry raw camera or lidar perception data; its role is strictly bounded to joint-level motor and sensor communication.

**EtherCAT On-the-Fly Ring Processing.** For high-axis-count systems (such as humanoids with 30 to 50 degrees of freedom), EtherCAT (ETG.1000) achieves deterministic 1 kHz to 10 kHz cycle times over standard 100BASE-TX full-duplex Ethernet ($R_{\text{link}} = 100\text{ Mbps}$). Rather than transmitting individual frames per axis, EtherCAT structures communication as an active logical ring:

1. The real-time master (executing on the safety microcontroller or `PREEMPT_RT` Linux host) transmits a single standard Ethernet frame (EtherType `0x88A4`) traversing all slave drives in a physical daisy chain.
2. Each drive integrates an EtherCAT Slave Controller (ESC) application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) (such as Beckhoff ET1100 or field-programmable gate array (FPGA) IP). As the frame's bits pass through the ESC's physical shift registers, the ESC **processes data on the fly**:
   - It reads commanded setpoints (joint target position, velocity, and feedforward torque) directly from its allocated byte offset in the datagram.
   - It writes actual measured feedback (encoder position, phase current, and drive status flags) into the moving frame.
3. The internal hardware processing latency per slave is strictly bounded ($t_{\text{slave},s} \approx 1.0\,\mu\text{s}$), and the frame is automatically looped back by the final slave on the second Ethernet pair.

The total round-trip cycle period for $S$ slave drives is bounded by:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \frac{B_{\text{frame}}}{R_{\text{link}}} + t_{\text{master}} + \sum_{s=1}^S t_{\text{slave},s} + t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{guard}} $$
For a 30-axis humanoid exchanging 8 bytes of command setpoints and 12 bytes of feedback per joint, the entire cyclic exchange ($600\text{ bytes}$) fits comfortably within a single $750\text{-byte}$ Ethernet frame. The complete round-trip across all 30 axes executes in approximately $65\,\mu\text{s}$ at $100\text{ Mbps}$, consuming less than $7\text{ percent}$ of the 1 ms control period. Furthermore, EtherCAT **Distributed Clocks (DC)** synchronize all slave timers to the master with sub-microsecond precision ($< 100\text{ ns}$ clock skew) by measuring and compensating for physical cable propagation delays, enabling synchronous PWM carrier generation across all inverter drives.

### Time-sensitive networking and scheduled ethernet gates

While EtherCAT processes frames on the fly through specialized slave controllers, modern multi-camera and lidar robotic systems require multi-gigabit Ethernet fabrics that transport high-bandwidth vision data alongside hard real-time actuator commands. IEEE **Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN)** provides deterministic Ethernet via standards that bound queuing jitter and reserve transmission windows:\index{Fieldbus!Time-Sensitive Networking}\index{Time-Sensitive Networking!Time-Aware Shaper}\index{Time-Sensitive Networking!frame preemption}

**IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Aware Shaper (TAS).** TAS coordinates traffic transmission using hardware-controlled transmission gates associated with each priority egress queue (traffic classes 0 to 7). A cyclic **Gate Control List (GCL)**—synchronized across all network bridges via IEEE 802.1AS (generalized Precision Time Protocol)—switches gates open or closed at precise physical time epochs. By reserving dedicated time windows exclusively for high-priority Scheduled Traffic (ST), TAS eliminates queuing interference from lower-priority Best-Effort (BE) traffic.

**Guard Bands and Frame Preemption.** Standard Ethernet frames are non-preemptive: once a transmission begins, it cannot be interrupted on physical copper or optical links. If a lower-priority best-effort packet begins transmission immediately before an ST time slice opens, the scheduled frame experiences transmission blocking of up to the maximum frame duration. To prevent this, TAS enforces a **guard band** prior to each scheduled traffic window:
$$ t_{\text{guard}} = \frac{\text{MTU}_{\text{BE}}}{R_{\text{link}}} $$
where $\text{MTU}_{\text{BE}}$ is the maximum transmission unit of best-effort traffic (typically 1,518 bytes, or 9,000 bytes for jumbo frames) and $R_{\text{link}}$ is the physical link bit rate. For a standard 1,518-byte frame on a 1 Gbps link, the guard band lasts:
$$ t_{\text{guard}} = \frac{1518 \times 8\text{ bits}}{10^9\text{ bps}} \approx 12.14\,\mu\text{s} $$
During this guard band, no best-effort frame may begin transmission if it cannot finish before the scheduled gate opens. This creates idle transmission overhead on the physical bus.

To reclaim this unused bandwidth, **IEEE 802.1Qbu and IEEE 802.3br Frame Preemption** divide preemptible (best-effort) MAC frames into fragments of at least 64 bytes. When an express (scheduled) frame arrives, the physical layer interrupts the ongoing preemptible frame, transmits the express frame with minimal latency, and resumes the preempted frame with an mPacket continuation header. Frame preemption reduces the maximum guard band from an entire MTU down to the minimum fragment size:
$$ t_{\text{guard,preempt}} = \frac{123\text{ bytes} \times 8\text{ bits}}{R_{\text{link}}} \approx 0.98\,\mu\text{s} $$
at 1 Gbps, reclaiming more than 90 percent of the lost guard band bandwidth and ensuring that multi-gigabit camera streaming does not inject millisecond-scale jitter into joint actuator control loops.

**Fieldbus Protocol Comparative Matrix.** @Tbl-fieldbus-comparative-synthesis contrasts the architectural attributes, latency bounds, and scaling ceilings across the four primary real-time communication protocols:

| Attribute / Metric           | CAN 2.0B (ISO 11898-1)               | CAN-FD (ISO 11898-1:2015)                | EtherCAT (ETG.1000)                      | IEEE TSN (802.1Qbv / 802.1Qbu)          |
|:-----------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|
| **Physical Layer**           | Differential twisted pair            | Differential twisted pair                | 100BASE-TX full-duplex Ethernet          | 1000BASE-T / 10GBASE-T switched Eth     |
| **Physical Topology**        | Linear multidrop bus                 | Linear multidrop bus                     | Daisy-chain / logical ring               | Switched star / tree / mesh             |
| **Raw Line Bit Rate**        | $1\text{ Mbps}$ max                  | $1\text{ Mbps}$ arb / $2\text{--}8\text{ Mbps}$ data | $100\text{ Mbps}$ full-duplex            | $1\text{--}10\text{ Gbps}$ full-duplex  |
| **Maximum Payload (MTU)**    | $8\text{ bytes}$                     | $64\text{ bytes}$                        | Up to $1486\text{ bytes}$ per datagram   | $1500\text{ bytes}$ ($9000\text{ B}$ jumbo) |
| **Arbitration Mechanism**    | Bitwise non-destructive priority     | Bitwise non-destructive with bit-rate switch | Hardware on-the-fly ESC processing      | Time-Aware Shaper (GCL) + frame preemption |
| **Worst-Case Jitter**        | $100\text{--}400\,\mu\text{s}$       | $50\text{--}200\,\mu\text{s}$            | $< 1.0\,\mu\text{s}$                     | $< 5.0\,\mu\text{s}$                    |
| **Hardware Clock Sync**      | None (asynchronous bit edges)        | None (asynchronous bit edges)            | Distributed Clocks (DC, $< 100\text{ ns}$) | IEEE 802.1AS gPTP ($< 100\text{ ns}$)   |
| **Max Axes at 1 kHz**        | $4\text{--}6\text{ axes}$            | $10\text{--}15\text{ axes}$              | $> 64\text{ axes}$                       | $> 100\text{ axes}$ (multiplexed with vision) |
| **Primary Robotic Domain**   | Auxiliary sensors, low-rate IO       | Quadruped leg clusters, gripper drives   | Multi-axis humanoids, surgical arms      | Sensor fusion ingress + safety backbone |

: **Comprehensive Architectural Synthesis of Real-Time Fieldbus Protocols**: Comparison of CAN 2.0B, CAN-FD, EtherCAT, and IEEE TSN across physical layer, framing, arbitration, jitter, and multi-axis control capacity. {#tbl-fieldbus-comparative-synthesis tbl-colwidths="[18,20,20,21,21]"}

**Fieldbus Cycle Budget Synthesis.** The achievable control cycle period $T_{\text{cycle}}$ across these four fieldbus architectures reflects their distinct arbitration mechanisms:

* **CAN 2.0B**: Cycle time is constrained by serial frame durations and lower-priority blocking over 8-byte messages:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{axes}}} t_{\text{frame,CAN2.0B},i} + \max_{k \in lp} t_{\text{frame,CAN2.0B},k} + t_{\text{margin}} $$
* **CAN-FD**: Cycle time is constrained by dual-rate serialization and lower-priority blocking over up to 64-byte messages:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{axes}}} t_{\text{frame},i} + \max_{k \in lp} t_{\text{frame},k} + t_{\text{margin}} $$
* **EtherCAT**: Cycle time is constrained by on-the-fly ring forwarding across $S$ slave controllers:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge \sum_f \frac{B_f}{R_{\text{link}}} + t_{\text{master}} + \sum_{s=1}^S t_{\text{slave},s} + t_{\text{prop}} + t_{\text{guard}} $$
* **TSN (802.1Qbv)**: Cycle time partitions transmission into scheduled and best-effort windows bounded by network synchronization uncertainty:
$$ T_{\text{cycle}} \ge T_{\text{ST}} + t_{\text{guard}} + T_{\text{BE}} + \Delta_{\text{sync}} $$
where $\Delta_{\text{sync}}$ is the maximum clock synchronization skew across network bridges. See @sec-nervous-deterministic-fieldbuses, @sec-nervous-cadences, and @sec-nervous-fieldbus-architectures for hardware fieldbus selection across the nervous system.

### Lock-free seqlocks for multi-rate shared memory

When a producer updates multiword state read by a deadline-bound enforcer, waiting on a producer-held mutex can violate the reader's deadline. The single-slot mailbox in @algo-lock-free-trajectory uses a sequence counter to detect a torn snapshot.

A **sequence counter** marks a single writer's publication in progress with an odd value and a completed publication with an even value:\index{Concurrency!sequence locks}

1. **Writer Protocol**:
   - Publish an odd sequence value, write the payload, and make it visible through the platform's coherent or cache-maintained memory contract.
   - Publish the next even value with release ordering.
2. **Reader Protocol**:
   - Read $S_1$ with acquire ordering. If it is odd, reject this publication without waiting.
   - Make one bounded copy to scratch memory using the platform's required load ordering, then read $S_2$.
   - Accept only if $S_1=S_2$ and both are even, and the copied frame passes integrity, timestamp, and lease checks. Otherwise retain the last validated local command only while its lease and stopping margin permit; then enter the state-matched fallback.

The reader's one-attempt execution time can be bounded on the target hardware; success probability depends on the writer's schedule and cannot be inferred from payload size alone. Conventional Linux seqlock readers may retry, as the [kernel documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/locking/seqlock.html) shows, but a real-time permission gate cannot use an unbounded retry loop.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-lock-free-trajectory
#| pdf-line-number: true
#| pdf-right-comment: false
#| html-comment-delimiter: "▷"

\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Single-Slot Trajectory Seqlock Baseline}
\begin{algorithmic}
\Require proposal $P$ (proposal header with $\text{sequence\_id}$, $\text{t\_evidence\_ns}$, $\text{sync\_error\_ns}$, $\text{t\_expire\_ns}$; waypoints $\mathbf{w}_{1..K}$; $\text{crc32}$), scratch buffer $B_{\text{scratch}}$ and previously validated active spline $B_{\text{active}}$ in static SRAM, shared SRAM mailbox $(c_{\text{seq}}, \text{Slot}_{\text{shared}})$, current time $t_{\text{now}}$ and evidence-age budget $t_{\text{age,max}}$ (the largest admissible $t_{\text{age}}$), both on the safety microcontroller's clock
\Ensure promoted validated chunk in $B_{\text{active}}$ or rejection with $B_{\text{active}}$ unchanged
\Statex
\Function{PublishActionChunk}{$P$}
    \State $c_{\text{curr}} \gets \Call{AtomicLoadExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_relaxed}}$
    \State $\Call{AtomicStoreExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, c_{\text{curr}} + 1, \text{memory\_order\_relaxed}}$ \Comment{mark odd: write in progress}
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSHST}}$ \Comment{outer-shareable store barrier pushes counter}
    \State $\Call{CopyMemory}{\text{Slot}_{\text{shared}}.\text{payload}, P, \text{sizeof}(P)}$ \Comment{copy multi-word trajectory}
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSH}}$ \Comment{outer-shareable full barrier: payload visible}
    \State $\Call{AtomicStoreExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, c_{\text{curr}} + 2, \text{memory\_order\_release}}$ \Comment{mark even: publish committed}
\EndFunction
\Statex
\Function{LatchLatestActionChunk}{$B_{\text{scratch}}, B_{\text{active}}, t_{\text{now}}$}
    \State $c_{\text{start}} \gets \Call{AtomicLoadExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_acquire}}$ \Comment{load initial counter (ARM LDAR acquire)}
    \If{$c_{\text{start}}$ is odd}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_WRITER\_ACTIVE}$ \Comment{writer active; retain prior spline}
    \EndIf
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSHLD}}$ \Comment{explicit barrier: prevent payload reads hoisting before counter}
    \State $\Call{CopyMemory}{B_{\text{scratch}}, \text{Slot}_{\text{shared}}.\text{payload}, \text{sizeof}(\text{Payload})}$ \Comment{tentative copy; active spline unchanged}
    \State $\Call{HardwareMemoryBarrier}{\text{DMB\_OSHLD}}$ \Comment{LDAR cannot prevent prior reads sinking; DMB forces payload reads before $c_{\text{end}}$}
    \State $c_{\text{end}} \gets \Call{AtomicLoadExplicit}{c_{\text{seq}}, \text{memory\_order\_acquire}}$ \Comment{re-read sequence counter}
    \If{$c_{\text{start}} \ne c_{\text{end}}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_TORN\_READ}$ \Comment{concurrent write detected}
    \EndIf
    \If{$\Call{ComputeCrc32}{B_{\text{scratch}}} \ne B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{crc32}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_CHECKSUM\_INVALID}$
    \EndIf
    \If{$t_{\text{now}} \ge B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{t\_expire\_ns}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_LEASE\_EXPIRED}$ \Comment{expiry is absolute; the reader may only shorten it}
    \EndIf
    \If{$t_{\text{now}} - B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{t\_evidence\_ns} + B_{\text{scratch}}.\text{sync\_error\_ns} > t_{\text{age,max}}$}
        \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_EVIDENCE\_STALE}$ \Comment{conversion error is added to every age}
    \EndIf
    \State $B_{\text{active}} \gets B_{\text{scratch}}$ \Comment{promote only after sequence, CRC, expiry, and evidence-age checks}
    \State \Return $\text{STATUS\_VALID\_LATCHED}$
\EndFunction
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

@Sec-nervous-cadences exchanges the proposal header and its chunk payload through this mailbox; @sec-appendix-systems-wire-header gives their byte layout.

## Camera Projective Geometry and Covariance Propagation {#sec-appendix-systems-vision}

In computer vision for machine learning, neural models typically process normalized pixel tensors to predict 2D bounding boxes or semantic segmentation masks. In physical AI systems, however, visual observations must be grounded as physical objects in continuous Euclidean 3D metric space to evaluate spatial clearance buffers $D_{\text{clear}}$ and enforce collision-avoidance invariants. Perception pipelines map continuous Euclidean 3D scenes onto discrete 2D camera photosite grids, and unproject pixel detections back into metric space under quantified measurement uncertainty.

### Intrinsic projection matrix and radial distortion

Under the standard pinhole camera model, a 3D point $\mathbf{p}_c = [x_c, y_c, z_c]^\top$ in camera coordinates projects onto pixel coordinates $\mathbf{u} = [u, v]^\top$ via the intrinsic calibration matrix $\mathbf{K}$:[^fn-sys-pinhole-projection]
$$
\tilde{\mathbf{u}} = \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{z_c} \mathbf{K} \mathbf{p}_c = \frac{1}{z_c} \begin{bmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_c \\ y_c \\ z_c \end{bmatrix}
$$
where $(f_x, f_y)$ are focal lengths in pixel units and $(c_x, c_y)$ is the principal point. Non-linear radial lens distortion is modeled by distortion coefficients $(k_1, k_2)$:
$$ r^2 = x_n^2 + y_n^2, \quad x_d = x_n (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4), \quad y_d = y_n (1 + k_1 r^2 + k_2 r^4) $$
where $(x_n, y_n) = (x_c / z_c, y_c / z_c)$ are normalized image coordinates.

[^fn-sys-pinhole-projection]: **Pinhole Intrinsic Projection**\index{Camera model!pinhole projection}: The pinhole model projects 3D points onto a 2D sensor through calibrated intrinsics. Under fixed pixel noise, the lateral variance after depth unprojection grows with squared distance; depth-error and calibration terms follow their own models. Uncalibrated intrinsics can bias a clearance estimate and must be included in its error envelope.

### Metric unprojection and spatial covariance propagation

When unprojecting a 2D pixel observation $\mathbf{u} = [u, v]^\top$ with measured depth $z$ into 3D camera coordinates, photosite measurement noise $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}} = \text{diag}(\sigma_u^2, \sigma_v^2, \sigma_z^2)$ propagates through the unprojection Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}$:\index{Mathematics!covariance propagation}
$$
\mathbf{p}_c = \begin{bmatrix} (u - c_x) z / f_x \\ (v - c_y) z / f_y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_c}{\partial [u, v, z]} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{z}{f_x} & 0 & \frac{u - c_x}{f_x} \\ 0 & \frac{z}{f_y} & \frac{v - c_y}{f_y} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
The propagated camera-frame spatial covariance is:
$$ \mathbf{\Sigma}_c = \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}} \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{meas}} \mathbf{J}_{\text{unproj}}^\top $$
Evaluating the diagonal terms shows that lateral positional variance along the camera $X$-axis scales with the square of depth:
$$ \sigma_{x_c}^2 \approx \left(\frac{z}{f_x}\right)^2 \sigma_u^2 + \left(\frac{u - c_x}{f_x}\right)^2 \sigma_z^2 $$
Because the leading term scales with $z^2$, spatial position uncertainty expands quadratically with distance. Transforming this 3D point into the robot body frame via rigid extrinsic transform $\mathbf{T}_{bc} = [\mathbf{R}_{bc}, \mathbf{p}_{bc}; \mathbf{0}^\top, 1]$ yields the spatial body covariance:
$$ \mathbf{\Sigma}_b = \mathbf{R}_{bc} \mathbf{\Sigma}_c \mathbf{R}_{bc}^\top + \mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}} $$
where $\mathbf{\Sigma}_{\text{ext}}$ models independent extrinsic uncertainty under this first-order approximation; correlations require the corresponding cross terms. A probabilistic clearance buffer may scale with $\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{\Sigma}_b)}$ at a declared tail risk. A deterministic permission check instead needs a justified bounded-error envelope; covariance alone does not give a worst-case bound.

### Zhang's planar homography and camera calibration

Zhang's calibration technique computes the camera intrinsic matrix $\mathbf{K}$ by observing a planar calibration rig (such as a checkerboard pattern) across $N \ge 3$ distinct orientations [@zhang2000flexible]. Without loss of generality, assume the model plane lies on $Z = 0$ in world coordinates. A 3D model point $\mathbf{M} = [X, Y, 0, 1]^\top$ maps to a 2D image point $\tilde{\mathbf{u}} = [u, v, 1]^\top$ through a $3 \times 3$ planar homography matrix $\mathbf{H}$:\index{Zhang's calibration!homography matrix}\index{Camera calibration!absolute conic}
$$
s \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{r}_1 & \mathbf{r}_2 & \mathbf{r}_3 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{r}_1 & \mathbf{r}_2 & \mathbf{t} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{H} \begin{bmatrix} X \\ Y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$
where $\mathbf{H} = [\mathbf{h}_1 \; \mathbf{h}_2 \; \mathbf{h}_3] = \lambda \mathbf{K} [\mathbf{r}_1 \; \mathbf{r}_2 \; \mathbf{t}]$ with arbitrary nonzero scalar $\lambda$.

#### Orthogonality constraints on the absolute conic

Because the rotation vectors $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ are orthonormal columns of an $SO(3)$ matrix ($\mathbf{r}_1^\top \mathbf{r}_2 = 0$ and $\|\mathbf{r}_1\| = \|\mathbf{r}_2\| = 1$), inverting $\mathbf{K}$ yields:
$$
\mathbf{r}_1 = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_1, \quad \mathbf{r}_2 = \frac{1}{\lambda} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_2
$$
Imposing orthonormality on $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$ defines two fundamental algebraic constraints per homography:
$$
\mathbf{h}_1^\top \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_2 = 0
$$
$$
\mathbf{h}_1^\top \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_1 - \mathbf{h}_2^\top \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1} \mathbf{h}_2 = 0
$$
The symmetric matrix $\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{K}^{-\top} \mathbf{K}^{-1}$ represents the image of the absolute conic (IAC):
$$
\mathbf{B} = \begin{bmatrix} B_{11} & B_{12} & B_{13} \\ B_{12} & B_{22} & B_{23} \\ B_{13} & B_{23} & B_{33} \end{bmatrix}
$$
Defining the 6-vector $\mathbf{b} = [B_{11}, B_{12}, B_{22}, B_{13}, B_{23}, B_{33}]^\top$, each quadratic term $\mathbf{h}_i^\top \mathbf{B} \mathbf{h}_j$ can be rewritten as the linear inner product $\mathbf{v}_{ij}^\top \mathbf{b}$, where:
$$
\mathbf{v}_{ij} = \begin{bmatrix} h_{i1}h_{j1} \\ h_{i1}h_{j2} + h_{i2}h_{j1} \\ h_{i2}h_{j2} \\ h_{i3}h_{j1} + h_{i1}h_{j3} \\ h_{i3}h_{j2} + h_{i2}h_{j3} \\ h_{i3}h_{j3} \end{bmatrix}
$$
The two constraints per observed orientation become the linear system:
$$
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v}_{12}^\top \\ (\mathbf{v}_{11} - \mathbf{v}_{22})^\top \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}
$$
Stacking $N \ge 3$ images forms the homogeneous system $\mathbf{V} \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}$, where $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{2N \times 6}$. The right singular vector of $\mathbf{V}$ corresponding to the smallest singular value provides $\mathbf{b}$ up to a scale factor. The intrinsic parameters $(f_x, f_y, c_x, c_y)$ and skew $\gamma$ are then uniquely extracted via Cholesky factorization of $\mathbf{B}$. This closed-form linear solution initializes the non-linear Levenberg–Marquardt optimization minimizing reprojection residuals over all observed fiducial corners.

## Kinematic Stopping Envelopes and Information Age Lag {#sec-appendix-systems-stopping}

In distributed systems, pipeline latency represents elapsed waiting time or queuing delay. In physical AI, end-to-end software latency converts directly into irreversible physical displacement—uninspected "blind travel"—during which an embodied machine traverses space with undiminished momentum before actuators can begin retarding motion. Halting an embodied machine transporting mass $m$ at velocity $v$ requires balancing sensorimotor information freshness, neural compute budgets, and fieldbus dispatch against physical mechanical braking deceleration.

### Sensorimotor information age and lag distance

For a specified hazard detector and stop path, let $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ bound the time from the physical state represented by the evidence until validated braking deceleration begins:\index{Kinematic stopping distance!observation age}
$$ \tau_{\text{delay}} = t_{\text{age}} + t_{\text{detect}} + t_{\text{compute}} + T_{\text{bus}} + T_{\text{act}} $$
where:

- $t_{\text{age}}$ converts the evidence timestamp to the controller clock and includes exposure/readout and clock error.
- $t_{\text{detect}}$ bounds recognition or lease-expiry detection.
- $t_{\text{compute}}$ is the admitted stop decision, including any required input transfer.
- $T_{\text{bus}}$ bounds command dispatch and network queuing.
- $T_{\text{act}}$ ends when the measured actuator begins delivering the specified deceleration, not when a command register is written.

Under the explicit simplifying assumption that speed cannot increase before brake onset, the blind travel is bounded by $d_{\text{blind}}=v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}$. If propulsion or a slope can increase speed, use its validated acceleration bound in this interval instead.

### Braking dynamics and friction limits

Tire-floor friction and actuator torque place upper limits on achievable deceleration; $a\le\mu g$ does not establish what braking the machine will deliver.\index{Braking!friction limit} Let $a_{\text{brake}}>0$ be a validated lower bound on *achieved* deceleration throughout the stop, for the declared load, temperature, slope, brake condition, and surface. A justified friction floor $\mu_{\text{floor}}$ may support that bound, but does not replace brake tests. With constant or stronger braking after onset, a localization bound $\delta_{\text{loc}}$, a fixed protective clearance $\delta_{\text{margin}}$, and a tracking-error bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$,
$$ d_{\text{stop}}(v)=v\,\tau_{\text{delay}}+\frac{v^2}{2a_{\text{brake}}}+\delta_{\text{loc}}+\delta_{\text{margin}}+\epsilon_{\text{track}}. $$
Motion is admitted only when $d_{\text{stop}}(v)\le D_{\text{clear}}$, where $D_{\text{clear}}$ is taken as a validated lower bound on available path clearance. This is the inset stopping distance that @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes defends. The sampled controller must reserve intersample travel and a state-matched stop before the viable region is lost.

### Kinetic energy derating and friction collapse

In an ideal friction-limited model, lowering $\mu$ from $\mu_{\text{nom}}$ to a positive $\mu_{\text{fault}}$ changes the braking-distance ratio to $\mu_{\text{nom}}/\mu_{\text{fault}}$.\index{Velocity clamp!kinetic derating} That ratio is illustrative; actual deceleration can also be limited by brake hardware or control. If surface friction is not sensed in time, derive $a_{\text{brake}}$ from a controlled surface condition and inspection schedule, exclude degraded surfaces, or withhold motion. For the constant-speed pre-brake model above, solving the clearance inequality gives
$$ v_{\text{clamp}}=-a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}}+\sqrt{(a_{\text{brake}}\tau_{\text{delay}})^2+2a_{\text{brake}}\left(D_{\text{clear}}-\delta_{\text{loc}}-\delta_{\text{margin}}-\epsilon_{\text{track}}\right)}. $$
This clamp is valid only when $D_{\text{clear}}$ exceeds the three fixed allowances, the braking and timing lower bounds hold, and the speed bound is enforced before entering the hazard corridor. No positive clamp follows if the available deceleration floor is unknown or zero.

## Wire Formats for the Record Chain {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-formats}

In distributed machine learning systems, inter-service contracts are defined via serialization frameworks such as Protocol Buffers, FlatBuffers, or JSON schemas, which rely on variable-length wire formats, dynamic deserialization, pointer indirection, and heap allocation. In physical AI systems, however, records crossing the causal boundary between unprivileged deep learning runtimes (executing in user space under Linux on 64-bit application processors) and certified real-time safety monitors (executing on 32-bit lockstep microcontrollers or RTOS partitions) must satisfy strict embedded systems invariants:\index{Serialization!wire formats}\index{Memory layout!natural alignment}\index{Zero-allocation!embedded contract chain}\index{Safety contract chain!14-record lineage}\index{Hardware exceptions!unaligned access trap}

1. *Zero Dynamic Allocation Invariant*: Deserialization must never invoke dynamic memory managers (`malloc`, `free`, C++ `new`, `delete`). Dynamic heap allocators manage internal free-list bins, take global allocator mutexes, and suffer from heap fragmentation. Under memory pressure, heap operations can invoke the `brk()` or `mmap()` system calls, triggering kernel memory compaction or page faults that stall execution for tens of milliseconds. In hard real-time control, all record slots, mailbox staging areas, scratch buffers, and circular telemetry logs must be statically sized at compile time and preallocated in dedicated static SRAM or Data Tightly Coupled Memory (DTCM) pools.
2. *Deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1)$ Parse Time*: Wire formats eliminate variable-length fields and pointer chasing. Every scalar and vector resides at a fixed, deterministic byte offset, allowing safety enforcers to inspect bounds, timestamps, and signatures in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ time with cycle-bounded instruction counts.
3. *Natural Alignment Across Heterogeneous ABIs*: On heterogeneous SoCs combining 64-bit application processors (ARM Cortex-A or x86_64) and 32-bit real-time microcontrollers (ARM Cortex-R52 or Cortex-M7), data types must be naturally aligned. A scalar of size $k$ bytes must reside at an offset satisfying:
$$ \text{offset} \equiv 0 \pmod k $$
Specifically, 64-bit timestamps and integers (`uint64_t`, `float64`) align on 8-byte boundaries ($k=8$), 32-bit values (`uint32_t`, `float32`) align on 4-byte boundaries ($k=4$), and 16-bit integers (`uint16_t`) align on 2-byte boundaries ($k=2$).

**Microarchitectural Consequences of Alignment Violations.** In certified safety microcontrollers (ISO 26262 ASIL D, IEC 61508 SIL 3), unaligned memory accesses are strictly forbidden. The system configuration register enables unaligned traps (`SCB->CCR |= SCB_CCR_UNALIGN_TRP_Msk`), causing any unaligned halfword or word access to raise an immediate `UsageFault` hardware exception that halts the processor. Even on cores where unaligned accesses are supported in hardware, an unaligned 32-bit or 64-bit access that crosses a 32-bit bus word or 64-byte cache-line boundary splits the memory transaction into multiple bus beats across the AXI/AHB-Lite interconnect. If an interrupt or another bus master intervenes between these beats, the access is torn, destroying single-cycle memory atomicity and corrupting lock-free seqlocks. Furthermore, compilers insert architecture-dependent padding bytes if structs contain unaligned members, producing binary layout discrepancies between 64-bit (AAPCS64) and 32-bit (AAPCS32) compilers. By declaring all padding explicitly as zero-filled `reserved` bytes, wire formats guarantee identical bit-level memory layouts across all compilers and processor cores.

**The 14-Record Safety Contract Chain.** Across this book, the physical AI machine stack maintains an unbroken chain of 14 formal cyber-physical contracts that govern execution from raw electromechanics up to legal release certification:

1. *Body Limit Record* (Contract 1, Body): Declares physical electromechanical envelopes (peak currents, torque limits, thermal $I^2 t$ constants, bus voltage limits, and gear ratios; @sec-body-actuator-limits).
2. *Proposal Record* (Contract 2, Brain): Emits candidate unprivileged kinematic trajectory setpoints across the proposal boundary (@sec-brain, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-header).
3. *Transport Budget / Handoff Record* (Contract 3, Nervous System): Specifies network cadences, clock domains, and sensor aging budgets ($\mathcal{H}_1$) across heterogeneous compute nodes (@sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix).
4. *Demonstration Provenance Record* (Contract 4, Data): Binds physical data collection conditions, sensor calibration revisions, plant serial numbers, and scenario ledgers to training datasets (@sec-data-policy-coverage).
5. *Policy Manifest* (Contract 5, Training): Cryptographically binds model architecture, quantization precision, network weight digests, and training distribution bounds (@sec-training-policy-manifest).
6. *Evaluation Record* (Contract 6, Evaluation): Summarizes statistical qualification trials across the operational design domain (ODD) and configures runtime monitor specifications (@sec-evaluation).
7. *Perception Evidence Record* (Contract 7, Perception): Encapsulates sensor observations with hardware capture epochs, clock conversion bounds, and spatial unprojection covariances (@sec-perception).
8. *Scene Memory State Record* (Contract 8, Memory): Maintains persistent spatial beliefs, tracked object bounds, volumetric occupancy fields, and invalidation deadlines across occlusions (@sec-memory).
9. *Intent Specification / Lease* (Contract 9, Intent): Formalizes admitted semantic goals, task tolerance boxes, wrench limits, and execution lease horizons (@sec-intent, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-intent).
10. *Trajectory Contract / Plan Record* (Contract 10, Planning): Packages admitted dynamic splines, knot point cadences, commit deadlines ($t_{\text{commit}}$), and emergency stop suffixes (@sec-planning, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-trajectory).
11. *Admitted Command Record / Enforcement Record* (Contract 11, Enforcement): Emits verified execution tokens, Control Barrier Function margins ($h(\mathbf{x})$), and tracking error ceilings ($\epsilon_{\text{track}}$) to actuator drives (@sec-enforcement, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-enforcement).
12. *Placement Record / Deployment Envelope* (Contract 12, Placement): Documents execution core affinities, memory interconnect QoS arbitration, loaded WCET bounds, and hardware isolation invariants (@sec-placement, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-placement).
13. *Authority Record / Forensic Log* (Contract 13, Intervention): Logs operator handover commands, bumpless transfer blending coefficients ($\alpha$), and tamper-evident cryptographic hash chains (@sec-intervention, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-authority).
14. *Verification Matrix / Release Manifest* (Contract 14, Verification & Release): Provides signed cryptographic attestation binding hardware root of trust anchors, adjudicator verdicts, fault injection trial ledgers, and residual-claims registers (@sec-verification, @sec-release, @sec-appendix-systems-wire-release).

Online runtime records (Contracts 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, and 13) travel across high-frequency shared SRAM mailboxes and real-time fieldbuses, requiring fixed-size layouts and zero dynamic allocation. Configuration and offline assurance artifacts (Contracts 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, and 14) are bound cryptographically by SHA-256 digests of their canonical binary encodings. All records use standard little-endian byte ordering for multi-byte scalars (`uint64_t`, `uint32_t`, `uint16_t`, `float32`, `float64`). Lineage is established by embedding parent SHA-256 digests, runtime corruption is caught via IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 checksums over headers and payloads, and operator authority is authenticated via HMAC-SHA-256 and Ed25519 digital signatures. Offline records (placement, fault, release) are identified by the SHA-256 digest of their canonical encoding, and the record that consumes one stores that digest under the consumed record's name.

### Proposal header and chunk payload {#sec-appendix-systems-wire-header}

Every proposal that crosses the proposal boundary opens with the same header, and `payload_kind` selects the payload that follows at `0x50`. @Tbl-appendix-systems-wire-header lays out the header with the minimal chunk payload of @sec-nervous-cadences. The chunk carries kinematic setpoints only. Torque is computed on the permission side, where the tracker derives it from the admitted reference, so a learned proposal never names a motor torque.
